Spatial aggregation: area-weighted estimation

Source: vignettes/theory-spatial-aggregation.qmd 
library(catchmentACS)
library(dplyr)
library(sf)

# Force network-free, deterministic builds: no provider/Census calls, no cache.
old_options <- options(
  catchmentACS.progress = "off",
  catchmentACS.rate_first_default = FALSE
)
old_cache <- getOption("catchmentACS.cache_enabled", NULL)
on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
on.exit(options(catchmentACS.cache_enabled = old_cache), add = TRUE)
cacs_set_cache(FALSE, scope = "session")

This article is a method-track companion to vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS"). The overview frames the whole pipeline as one estimator and states that a count and an average are aggregated by two different weights; this article derives that result and then does something the overview cannot — it reproduces the package’s arithmetic by hand, on a bundled fixture, so a methodologist can confirm that the formulas on this page are the formulas the code runs. It is written for a reader who wants the areal-interpolation model on the page: the uniform-within-tract assumption stated precisely, the coverage weight and the normalized mean weight built from first principles, the six estimand families laid out with the exact aggregation formula and the weight each one uses, and a numerical check that earns trust in the implementation. The reference page ?cacs_intersect_weight is the implementation anchor; this article supplies the mathematics behind its “Estimand families and weights” section.

We reuse the notation fixed in the overview without redefining its motivation: the isochrone I_s, the tract T_j, the intersection I_s \cap T_j, the equal-area measure \lvert\,\cdot\,\rvert, a count estimate Y_j, a scalar estimate X_j, and a rate’s numerator and denominator counts A_j, B_j. The two weights w^{cov}_{sj} and w^{mean}_{sj} and the three estimator forms \widehat{Y}_s, \widehat{\bar X}_s, \widehat{R}_s are restated where they are derived. The margin-of-error algebra is not developed here — it is the subject of vignette("theory-moe-propagation", package = "catchmentACS").

About the data in this article

The single numerical check below is built entirely from the package’s bundled inst/extdata fixtures — the synthetic legacy_2025_isochrones, legacy_2025_sites, and sample_alabama_subset objects — so this article renders with no Census, OSRM, ORS, or other network calls. These fixtures preserve the production calling contract (sites, drive-time polygons, tract-level ACS variables) but are synthetic and illustrative: they are included only for examples, tests, and reproducible package checks. They are not live Alabama policy estimates and must not be cited as real ACS results. Any real analysis requires a fresh live run (see vignette("providers", package = "catchmentACS")).

The areal-interpolation model

The estimand is a neighborhood characteristic of the population that lives inside a drive-time catchment I_s: the count of people in poverty within a 10-minute drive of a site, the per-capita income of that catchment, its SNAP rate. The ACS publishes its estimates on census tracts T_j, whose boundaries were drawn for enumeration, not for travel time. A drive-time area slices straight through tract edges, capturing some tracts whole and others only in part — a sliver of one, half of another, the whole of a third. Areal interpolation is the model that re-expresses a tract-level published value as a catchment-level value across that misalignment.

The model rests on a single assumption.

Uniform-within-tract assumption. The characteristic of interest is spread uniformly over the area of each tract T_j. A catchment covering 40% of a tract’s area contains 40% of whatever the tract counts.

Stated as a density, let \rho_j be the quantity of the characteristic per unit area in tract T_j. Uniformity means \rho_j is constant across T_j, so the amount of the characteristic contained in any sub-region S \subseteq T_j is proportional to that sub-region’s area,

\text{amount in } S = \rho_j \, \lvert S \rvert = \big(\text{tract amount}\big)\cdot\frac{\lvert S \rvert}{\lvert T_j \rvert}.

Taking S = I_s \cap T_j gives the amount of the characteristic the catchment captures from tract j: the tract’s published amount, scaled by the fraction of the tract’s area inside the catchment. That fraction is the coverage weight of the next section, and the whole estimator is built from this one identity.

The assumption’s reach depends on the type of variable, and the distinction is the hinge of everything that follows.

  • An extensive (count) variable, Y_j — persons, households, persons in poverty — is an amount that lives in the tract. Under uniformity it splits in proportion to area: half the tract’s area carries half its people. The model is exact for area and approximate for the count, the approximation being only as good as the uniformity of the underlying density.
  • An intensive (scalar) variable, X_j — a median, a per-capita figure, a rate expressed as a level — is a per-unit quantity, not an amount. It does not accumulate over area: half a tract does not hold “half a dollar of per-capita income.” Splitting an intensive value by area is meaningless. What the model can do for an intensive variable is treat its tract value as the local level of a field and form an area-weighted average of the tract values the catchment overlaps — a blend, not a sum.

This is exactly why one weight cannot serve both. Extensive variables are summed with a weight that allocates a fraction of each tract amount; intensive variables are averaged with a weight that is a share and sums to one. The package encodes this split as a variable’s estimand family; the two weights are the two ways the same intersection area enters an aggregate.

When the assumption fails. It is most strained where population is concentrated on a small part of a large tract. Suppose 80% of a tract’s area is uninhabited woodland and its residents are packed into the remaining 20%. A catchment that clips only the woodland edge gets a coverage weight near 0.8, and area weighting then credits the catchment with ~80% of the tract’s population — when the truth is closer to 0%. The error is largest where land use is most heterogeneous within a tract: the urban–rural fringe, coastlines, large rural tracts straddling a town and its hinterland. The reserved weight_method = "population" mode is designed to relax exactly this assumption by substituting an ancillary population surface for area as the allocation basis (a dasymetric refinement); in the current release area is the only basis, and the assumption is stated plainly rather than hidden. Everything below concerns the implemented area path, whose honest caveat is this paragraph.

Coverage weight versus normalized mean weight

Both weights are built from the same ingredient, the intersection area \lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert. They differ only in what they divide it by, and that single difference is the difference between a total and an average.

The coverage weight. From the areal-interpolation identity, the share of tract j’s amount that the catchment captures is the fraction of the tract’s area inside the catchment,

w^{cov}_{sj} = \frac{\lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert}{\lvert T_j \rvert} \;\in\; [0, 1].

It is bounded by one tract at a time: w^{cov}_{sj} = 1 when T_j \subseteq I_s (the tract is wholly inside the catchment) and w^{cov}_{sj} = 0 when the two are disjoint. Crucially, the coverage weights of the tracts a catchment touches do not sum to one. Summing over j,

\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} = \sum_j \frac{\lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert}{\lvert T_j \rvert} \;\neq\; 1

in general, because each term divides by a different tract area \lvert T_j \rvert. Its value is interpretable: it is the effective number of tract-equivalents the catchment covers. A catchment that wholly contained two tracts and half of a third would have \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} = 2.5; three tracts each half-covered would sum to about 1.5. Because the catchment area \lvert I_s \rvert equals \sum_j \lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert when I_s lies entirely within the tract layer, the coverage sum is the catchment’s area re-expressed in units of “average tract,” not a probability that must normalize. The package surfaces this sum directly as the weight_sum column, and a value near a small integer means the catchment captured roughly that many whole tracts.

The normalized mean weight. An intensive variable needs a share: each tract should contribute to the catchment average in proportion to how much of the catchment it accounts for, with the contributions summing to one. Dividing the intersection area by the total intersection area over the catchment gives

w^{mean}_{sj} = \frac{\lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert}{\sum_k \lvert I_s \cap T_k \rvert},

and this is normalized by construction,

\sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} = \frac{\sum_j \lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert}{\sum_k \lvert I_s \cap T_k \rvert} = 1,

because the numerator summed over j is exactly the denominator. The sum-to-one property is structural, not coincidental. The two weights are proportional within a catchment — w^{mean}_{sj} \propto w^{cov}_{sj}\, \lvert T_j \rvert — but they are renormalized against different denominators, and that is what separates a quantity that scales with the catchment from one that stays on the per-unit scale of the variable.

Why the families split this way. Put the two estimators side by side.

  • A count is a sum of amounts, so it is aggregated with the coverage weight:

    \widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, Y_j .

    If the catchment captures more area it captures more people, and \widehat{Y}_s grows accordingly. Using a normalized weight here would force the answer to a per-tract average and destroy the dependence on catchment size — a silent error.

  • A scalar is a per-unit level, so it is aggregated with the normalized mean weight as a convex combination of the tract values:

    \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj}\, X_j , \qquad \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} = 1 .

    Because the weights sum to one and are non-negative, \widehat{\bar X}_s lies between \min_j X_j and \max_j X_j: a catchment average per-capita income cannot exceed every tract’s per-capita income. Using the coverage weight here would let an intensive value accumulate past any tract’s level — again a silent error, not a runtime failure.

  • A derived rate is a ratio of two extensive quantities. Each of the numerator and denominator is aggregated as its own coverage-weighted total, and the ratio is formed last:

    \widehat{R}_s = \frac{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, A_j}{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, B_j} .

    The rate inherits the coverage path because both of its parts are counts; it is not a weighted average of tract rates, which would weight a tiny-denominator tract the same as a large one.

Neither misuse raises a warning. Apply the coverage weight to an intensive variable and you sum quantities that should average, producing a dollar figure inflated past any tract’s value — an income no one earns. Apply the mean weight to a count and you average quantities that should accumulate, producing a per-tract-ish number disconnected from how many people the catchment actually contains. The arithmetic runs; it just estimates the wrong thing. This is the silent estimand error the family classifier exists to prevent, and the reason the package refuses to apply one universal weight to every variable.

The numerical check at the end of this article exhibits both sums on real fixture geometry: \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} coming out to a non-integer, and \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} coming out to exactly one.

The six estimand families

A variable’s estimand family is the rule that selects its weight and its aggregation formula. The package classifies every requested ACS variable into one of six families up front, then dispatches the matching arithmetic, so applying the wrong weight to a variable cannot happen quietly. The table gives the point estimate and the weight for each; the margin-of-error column is deliberately omitted, as the MOE formulas are derived in the companion article.

Estimand family Representative variable Point-estimate aggregation Weight
spatial_total total population; persons in poverty (B17001_002) \widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} Y_j coverage w^{cov}_{sj}
derived_rate poverty rate; SNAP rate \widehat{R}_s = \dfrac{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} A_j}{\sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} B_j} coverage, numerator and denominator separately
area_weighted_scalar_proxy per-capita income (B19301_001) \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} X_j normalized mean w^{mean}_{sj}
population_weighted_scalar_proxy (reserved) scalar proxy under population weighting \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} X_j population-normalized mean
median_proxy tract median household income (B19013_001) weighted blend of tract medians, not the true catchment median normalized mean w^{mean}_{sj}
metadata_only provenance fields no numeric aggregation none

A few families need a word beyond the table.

spatial_total and derived_rate are the two coverage-weighted families. The total is the direct application of \widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} Y_j. The rate preserves the coverage-weighted numerator total \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} A_j and denominator total \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} B_j as separate carriers and divides them last, so it is a ratio of catchment totals rather than an average of tract ratios.

area_weighted_scalar_proxy is the active intensive family in this release: a convex combination of tract values under the normalized mean weight, on the same per-unit scale as the inputs. Its point estimate is, by definition, \widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj}\, X_j. The exact per-cell normalization the package applies when a single requested variable is missing in some intersecting tracts is the implementation’s responsibility, documented in ?cacs_intersect_weight; the definitional blend above always lands between the contributing tracts’ minimum and maximum.

population_weighted_scalar_proxy is a reserved family. It would replace the area-based mean weight with a population-based one, allocating by an ancillary population surface instead of by area to relax the uniform-within-tract assumption where population is concentrated. Conceptually this is dasymetric refinement: a finer ancillary layer (block-group population) is used to redistribute the coarser tract quantity, so the allocation follows people rather than land. In the current release this family is inert — weight_method = "population" stops with a clear error at the orchestrator boundary — and the population weight is not yet propagated through to estimates.

median_proxy carries an explicit caveat. A median is not additive and not averageable: the median of a pooled population is generally not any weighted average of the sub-populations’ medians, which would require the underlying income distribution the ACS does not publish at the tract level. The package reports a mean-weighted blend of the tract medians under w^{mean}_{sj} as a proxy, a convenient summary on the right scale, and labels it as such throughout. It is not the true median household income of the catchment population. The proxy is honest about being a proxy.

metadata_only variables are provenance fields that carry through without any numeric aggregation.

The classifier and the per-family dispatch are documented in the “Estimand families and weights” section of ?cacs_intersect_weight; this section is the derivation behind that documentation.

Why EPSG:5070

Both weights are ratios in which the intersection area appears. A ratio of areas is only meaningful if numerator and denominator are measured in the same metric, and only unbiased across the catchment if that metric preserves area everywhere — so that “fraction of the tract” behaves like a fraction wherever the tract falls on the map. That is precisely the property of an equal-area projection, and it is why the choice of coordinate reference system is part of the estimator’s correctness, not a display detail.

On a geographic CRS (longitude/latitude), area is either dimensionless (degrees-squared, which is not an area) or, with great-circle integration, an ellipsoidal figure that is not equal-area. Web Mercator inflates area away from the equator dramatically. None preserves the proportionality the weights rely on, so the same physical hectare would be measured as more land in one part of the map than another, and w^{cov}_{sj} would silently over- or under-credit tracts by where they sit, not by how much the catchment covers them. The package therefore transforms validated inputs once, before measuring any area, to EPSG:5070 (NAD83 / CONUS Albers Equal Area), an Albers equal-area projection whose standard parallels are placed so that areal distortion across the contiguous United States is held to a fraction of a percent — and across the Southeast, between the standard parallels, it is effectively nil. With areas measured on EPSG:5070, a square meter of intersection contributes the same weight in north and south, \lvert T_j \rvert and \lvert I_s \cap T_j \rvert are evaluated in the same \text{m}^2, and the coverage and mean weights mean what their formulas say. The choice also follows entrenched domain practice: equal-area CONUS Albers is the de facto standard for tract-level area work, which keeps these results comparable to neighboring analyses.

This is also the reason the current release is scoped to the contiguous United States plus DC: EPSG:5070 is the authoritative equal-area default there, where Albers distortion is negligible. Regions outside that footprint — Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico — would need a different equal-area CRS and are deferred to a future release. The single up-front transform happens before the per-site loop, and no re-projection occurs inside it, so every area in a run is comparable on the same equal-area metric.

Computation

The mathematics above is per-tract, but a run involves many sites and many tracts, and the implementation strategy is a deliberate choice rather than an incidental one. The package evaluates the estimator with a per-site loop: each site (and drive-time band) is processed in a closed body that subsets only that isochrone, prefilters candidate tracts with a spatial index, cuts the exact intersection geometry against only those candidates, measures intersection area and divides by the pre-computed tract area to get w^{cov}_{sj}, builds both weight columns, and aggregates by family — before moving to the next. The alternative — one large vectorized spatial join over the full site-by-tract cross-product — is rejected for two reasons that matter at scale.

  • Memory predictability. A single join would hold every intersection polygon in memory at once, so peak memory grows with the total number of intersections across all sites. The per-site loop’s working set is one catchment and its handful of overlapping tracts, so peak memory is independent of the number of sites and the largest study areas stay tractable.
  • Debugging and error isolation. Spatial intersection is sensitive to invalid geometry, and in a single join one bad polygon can abort the whole batch with a stack trace that does not say which input was at fault. In the loop, a failure is attributable to a specific site, and a site whose geometry cannot be repaired is marked with a missing result while the rest of the batch proceeds.

Two robustness concerns are handled at the level of the individual site.

Geometry repair. Tract polygons and provider isochrones often arrive with self-intersections, slivers, or holes that make an exact intersection throw a topology error. The package applies a tiered repair before intersecting: a quick validity check passes clean geometry through untouched; otherwise a standard make-valid step fixes the large majority of cases; and a last-resort zero-width buffer handles the remainder. Geometry that survives all three tiers still invalid is treated as a failure for that site rather than silently producing a wrong area.

Edge cases. A handful of geometric situations are handled explicitly, each isolated to the site where it occurs.

  • Empty intersection. A catchment that overlaps no tract — outside ACS coverage, or a missing isochrone — yields a result row marked as covering zero tracts, so the caller can detect it rather than mistake it for a real estimate of zero.
  • Sliver fragments. A tract clipped along a coastline or river can intersect in a fragment so thin that its weight is floating-point noise. A small min_weight threshold drops these negligible fragments before they enter an aggregate, so they cannot perturb a total.
  • Self-intersections. These are the geometry-repair case above, resolved by the tiered repair and, failing that, by isolating the site.

The conceptual point is that the loop turns batch-level fragility into site-level diagnosability, and the equal-area weights are computed identically inside it. The full parameter contract, the default min_weight, the audit attribute used below, and the per-row provenance live in ?cacs_intersect_weight.

Numerical verification: the formulas match the package

This is the section that earns a methodologist’s trust. We take one site and one ring from the fixtures, pull the per-tract audit the package exposes, and recompute the coverage weights and a spatial-total aggregation entirely by hand from the audit’s two area columns. Then we show the by-hand figures equal the package’s reported figures to machine precision. If the formulas on this page were not the formulas the code runs, this check would fail.

We deliberately pick a catchment whose coverage is partial and uneven — not a trivial fully-enclosed case — so the area-fraction formula is genuinely exercised and the coverage and mean weights are genuinely different. The synthetic site AL_SITE_17 at a 10-minute drive time intersects three tracts: one it fully contains and two it clips at the edge.

First, intersect and keep the per-tract audit:

# These fixtures are exactly the shapes pipeline stages 1-2 would have returned,
# frozen for offline reproducibility.
sites <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_sites.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))
iso <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "legacy_2025_isochrones.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))
acs <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "sample_alabama_subset.rds", package = "catchmentACS"
))

site_id    <- "AL_SITE_17"
drive_time <- 10L

iso_one <- iso[
  iso$site_id == site_id & iso$drive_time_min == drive_time, ,
  drop = FALSE
]

weighted <- cacs_intersect_weight(
  iso_sf           = iso_one,
  acs_sf           = acs,
  weight_method    = "area",
  keep_tract_audit = TRUE,
  verbose          = FALSE
)

The audit attribute holds, for each tract the catchment touched, the intersection area int_area_m2 and the full tract area tract_area_m2 — the two ingredients of w^{cov}_{sj} — both measured on EPSG:5070:

audit <- attr(weighted, "cacs_tract_audit") |>
  select(GEOID, int_area_m2, tract_area_m2) |>
  arrange(desc(int_area_m2))

audit
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID       int_area_m2 tract_area_m2
  <chr>             <dbl>         <dbl>
1 01125001001    9233961.      9233961.
2 01127001001    1038977.      9233961.
3 01123001001    1038971.      9233961.

Step 1 — recompute both weights by hand

From those two columns we form the coverage weight (each tract’s own denominator) and the normalized mean weight (the common catchment denominator), straight from the formulas above:

hand <- audit |>
  mutate(
    w_cov  = int_area_m2 / tract_area_m2,        # |I_s n T_j| / |T_j|
    w_mean = int_area_m2 / sum(int_area_m2)      # |I_s n T_j| / sum_k |I_s n T_k|
  )

hand |> select(GEOID, w_cov, w_mean)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID       w_cov w_mean
  <chr>       <dbl>  <dbl>
1 01125001001 1.000 0.816
2 01127001001 0.113 0.0918
3 01123001001 0.113 0.0918
c(
  sum_w_cov  = sum(hand$w_cov),    # NOT 1: each term has its own denominator
  sum_w_mean = sum(hand$w_mean)    # exactly 1 by construction
)
 sum_w_cov sum_w_mean
  1.225033   1.000000

The three coverage weights are 1.000, 0.1125, and 0.1125: one tract fully enclosed, two clipped to about a ninth of their area. Their sum, about 1.225, is the effective number of whole tracts the catchment covers — emphatically not one, exactly as the derivation said. The mean weights, by contrast, sum to exactly 1. That structural contrast is the entire difference between a total and an average, here in fixture numbers.

Step 2 — recompute a spatial total by hand

Now a count. Persons in poverty (B17001_002) is a spatial_total, so the package reports \widehat{Y}_s = \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj}\, Y_j. We pull the three tracts’ published counts and form that sum by hand:

counts <- acs |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(GEOID %in% hand$GEOID, variable == "B17001_002") |>
  select(GEOID, Y = estimate)

hand_total <- hand |>
  select(GEOID, w_cov) |>
  left_join(counts, by = "GEOID")

hand_total
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID       w_cov     Y
  <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>
1 01125001001 1.000  1020
2 01127001001 0.113  1104
3 01123001001 0.113   828
hand_Y_hat       <- sum(hand_total$w_cov * hand_total$Y)   # sum_j w_cov * Y_j
hand_weight_sum  <- sum(hand_total$w_cov)                  # sum_j w_cov

c(hand_Y_hat = hand_Y_hat, hand_weight_sum = hand_weight_sum)
     hand_Y_hat hand_weight_sum
    1237.382230        1.225033

Step 3 — compare against the package

The package’s own row for the same variable reports the estimate and the weight sum it computed internally:

pkg_row <- weighted |>
  filter(variable == "B17001_002") |>
  select(variable, estimate, weight_sum, n_tracts,
         estimand_family, weight_basis)

pkg_row
# A tibble: 1 × 6
  variable   estimate weight_sum n_tracts estimand_family weight_basis
  <chr>         <dbl>      <dbl>    <int> <chr>           <chr>
1 B17001_002    1237.       1.23        3 spatial_total   coverage

estimand_family is spatial_total and weight_basis is coverage, confirming the package routed this count through the coverage path. Now the equality check — by-hand against package, on both the estimate and the weight sum:

c(
  estimate_match      = isTRUE(all.equal(hand_Y_hat,      pkg_row$estimate)),
  weight_sum_match    = isTRUE(all.equal(hand_weight_sum, pkg_row$weight_sum)),
  estimate_abs_diff   = abs(hand_Y_hat      - pkg_row$estimate),
  weight_sum_abs_diff = abs(hand_weight_sum - pkg_row$weight_sum)
)
     estimate_match    weight_sum_match   estimate_abs_diff weight_sum_abs_diff
                  1                   1                   0                   0

Both match. The hand-computed spatial total — about 1237 persons in poverty — equals the package’s estimate, and the hand-computed \sum_j w^{cov}_{sj} equals the package’s weight_sum, with absolute differences at the floating-point floor (on the order of 10^{-12} and 10^{-15}). The weight_sum column the package reports is the not-equal-to-one coverage sum from Step 1, and the estimate is the coverage-weighted count we built from the audit. The formulas in this article and the arithmetic in the code are the same arithmetic.

The mean weight’s defining property is equally direct to confirm from the same audit:

# w_mean sums to exactly one within this (site, drive_time) cell.
isTRUE(all.equal(sum(hand$w_mean), 1))
[1] TRUE

The intensive path, by definition

A spatial_total count and an area_weighted_scalar_proxy scalar reuse this identical intersection geometry; only the denominator of the weight differs — \lvert T_j \rvert for the total just verified, \sum_k \lvert I_s \cap T_k \rvert for the mean. By definition the scalar proxy is the mean-weighted blend

\widehat{\bar X}_s = \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj}\, X_j ,

a convex combination that lands strictly between \min_j X_j and \max_j X_j. Because the mean weights just summed to one, this is the structural guarantee that a catchment “average per-capita income” cannot exceed any tract’s per-capita income — the exact opposite of what summing an intensive level with the coverage weight would do, which inflates the figure past every tract’s value into a number no one earns. That is the silent estimand error the family split exists to enforce, and it is why the package routes B19301_001 through the mean path and B17001_002 through the coverage path automatically.

The package’s reported proxy estimate for a scalar is on this per-unit scale by construction. Its exact per-cell normalization — in particular how it handles a requested variable that is missing in some intersecting tracts — is a bookkeeping detail that is the package’s responsibility, documented in the “Estimand families and weights” section of ?cacs_intersect_weight. We therefore frame the proxy here at the level of its definition rather than printing a specific proxy estimate number, so this self-contained check stays anchored on the coverage-weighted spatial_total path it verifies exactly, and on the \sum_j w^{mean}_{sj} = 1 identity, both confirmed above to machine precision.

To summarize the check: the coverage weight, its non-unit sum, the package’s weight_sum, and the coverage-weighted spatial_total all coincide with the hand computation to the floating-point floor; the mean weights sum to exactly one; and the scalar proxy is the definitional mean-weighted blend on the per-unit scale, between each tract’s minimum and maximum.

Where this sits

This article derived and verified the spatial half of the estimator. Its two companions cover the uncertainty half, and the methodology overview ties all three together; each reuses the notation fixed in the overview.

  • The estimator overview, with the shared notation, the six-family table, and the count-vs-average worked example: vignette("methodology", package = "catchmentACS"). This article is the derivation behind its weight and family sections.
  • MOE propagation — the published tract MOEs are carried through these same weights by cacs_propagate_moe(); the four formula families, the M = 1.645\,SE conversion, the ratio-variance forms, and the independence assumptions are derived in vignette("theory-moe-propagation", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_propagate_moe.
  • Derived rates — the coverage-weighted numerator and denominator totals built here are divided into the curated catchment rates in vignette("theory-derived-rates", package = "catchmentACS") and ?cacs_derive_rates.
  • Function reference — the locked signature, the per-site loop, the edge cases, the tract audit attribute used above, the min_weight sliver filter, the per-row provenance, and the “Estimand families and weights” section: ?cacs_intersect_weight.

For the applied, run-it path that produces reporting tables from these same fixtures, see vignette("getting-started", package = "catchmentACS") and vignette("alabama-tutorial", package = "catchmentACS").
